blocks.p: The Son of God presents to his Father the prayers of our first parents, now repenting, and intercedes for them. God accepts them, but declares that they must no longer live in Paradise, and sends Michael with a band of cherubim to dispossess them, but first to reveal future things to Adam. Michael comes down. Adam points out to Eve certain ominous signs; he sees Michael approaching and goes out to meet him. The Angel announces their departure. Eve laments. Adam pleads, but submits. The Angel leads him up a high hill and sets before him in a vision what shall happen until the Flood.

v: Thus they in lowliest plight repentant stood
Praying; for from the mercy seat above
Prevenient grace descending had removed
The stony from their hearts, and made new flesh
Regenerate grow instead, that sighs now breathed
Unutterable, which the Spirit of prayer
Inspired, and winged for Heaven with speedier flight
Than loudest oratory. Yet their mien
Was not of common suitors, nor less grave
Their plea appeared than when the ancient pair
In fables old, less ancient yet than these,
Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha, to restore
The drowned race of mankind, before the shrine
Of Themis stood devout. To Heaven their prayers
Flew up, nor missed the way, by envious winds
Blown vagabond or frustrate: in they passed
Dimensionless through heavenly doors; then, clad
With incense, where the golden altar fumed,
By their great Intercessor, came in sight
Before the Father’s throne. Them the glad Son
Presenting, thus to intercede began:
“See, Father, what first fruits on earth have sprung
From your implanted grace in Man: these sighs
And prayers, which in this golden censer, mixed
With incense, I your priest before you bring;
Fruits of more pleasing savor, from your seed
Sown with contrition in his heart, than those
Which his own hand, in tending all the trees
Of Paradise, could have produced, before
His fall from innocence. Now therefore bend
Your ear to pleading; hear his sighs, though mute;
Unskilled to know what words to pray, let me
Interpret for him, me his advocate
And propitiation; all his works on me,
Good or not good, engraft; my merit those
Shall perfect, and for these my death shall pay.
Accept me, and in me from these receive
The smell of peace toward mankind; let him live
Before you reconciled, at least his days
Numbered, though sad, till death, his doom (which I
To mitigate thus plead, not to reverse),
To better life shall yield him, where with me
All my redeemed may dwell in joy and bliss,
Made one with me as I with you am one.”
To whom the Father, without cloud, serene:
“All your request for Man, accepted Son,
Obtain; all your request was my decree.
But longer in that Paradise to dwell
The law I gave to nature him forbids:
Those pure immortal elements that know
No gross, no unharmonious mixture foul,
Eject him, tainted now, and purge him off
As a distemper, gross, to air as gross,
And mortal food, as may dispose him best
For dissolution wrought by Sin, that first
Distempered all things, and of incorrupt
Corrupted. I at first with two fair gifts
Created him endowed, with happiness
And immortality: that, rashly lost,
The other served but to make woe eternal,
Till I provided Death; so Death becomes
His final remedy, and, after life
Tried in sharp tribulation, and refined
By faith and faithful works, to second life,
Waked in the renovation of the just,
Resigns him up with Heaven and Earth renewed.
But let us call to synod all the blessed
Through Heaven’s wide bounds; from them I will not hide
My judgments, how with mankind I proceed,
As they saw lately with the sinning angels;
And in their state, though firm, stood more confirmed.”
He ended, and the Son gave signal high
To the bright minister that watched; he blew
His trumpet, heard on Horeb since, perhaps,
When God descended, and perhaps once more
To sound at general doom. The angelic blast
Filled all the regions: from their blissful bowers
Of amaranthine shade, fountain or spring,
By the waters of life, wherever they sat
In fellowships of joy, the sons of light
Hastened, repairing to the summons high,
And took their seats; till from his throne supreme
The Almighty thus pronounced his sovereign will:
“O sons, like one of us Man has become
To know both good and evil, since his taste
Of that forbidden fruit; but let him boast
His knowledge of good lost, and evil got,
Happier had it sufficed him to have known
Good by itself, and evil not at all.
He sorrows now, repents, and prays contrite,
My motions in him; longer than they move,
His heart I know, how variable and vain
Self-left. Lest therefore his now bolder hand
Reach also for the Tree of Life, and eat,
And live forever, dream at least to live
Forever, to remove him I decree,
And send him from the garden forth to till
The ground he was taken from, fitter soil.
Michael, I give this charge into your hands:
Take with you from among the cherubim
Your choice of flaming warriors, lest the Fiend,
Either on Man’s behalf, or to invade
An empty holding, raise some new unrest.
Make haste, and from the Paradise of God
Without remorse drive out the sinful pair,
From hallowed ground the unholy, and proclaim
To them and to their progeny from there
Perpetual banishment. Yet, lest they faint
At the sad sentence rigorously pressed
(For I behold them softened, and with tears
Bewailing their excess), all terror hide.
If patiently they follow your command,
Dismiss them not disconsolate; reveal
To Adam what shall come in future days,
As I shall give you light; and intermix
My covenant in the woman’s seed renewed;
So send them forth, though sorrowing, yet in peace.
And on the east side of the garden place,
Where entrance up from Eden easiest climbs,
A cherub watch, and of a sword the flame
Wide-waving, to scare off all approach afar,
And guard all passage to the Tree of Life,
Lest Paradise a harboring place should prove
For spirits foul, and all my trees their prey,
With stolen fruit to fool mankind once more.”
He ceased; and the archangelic Power prepared
For swift descent, with him the cohort bright
Of watchful cherubim; four faces each
Had, like a double Janus; all their shape
Spangled with eyes more numerous than those
Of Argus, and more wakeful than to drowse,
Charmed by the pipe of Arcady, the reed
Of Hermes, or his opiate rod. Meanwhile,
To greet the world again with sacred light,
Leucothea woke, and with fresh dews embalmed
The earth, when Adam and first matron Eve
Had ended now their morning prayers, and found,
Strength added from above, new hope to spring
Out of despair, joy, though with fear still linked;
And so to Eve he spoke his welcome words:
“Eve, easily may faith admit that all
The good which we enjoy from Heaven descends;
But that from us something should rise to Heaven
So strong in pleading as to move the mind
Of God on high, or to incline his will,
Hard to believe may seem; yet this will prayer,
Or one short sigh of human breath, borne up
Even to the seat of God. For since I sought
By prayer the offended Deity to appease,
Knelt and before him humbled all my heart,
I thought I saw him placable and mild,
Bending his ear; persuasion in me grew
That I was heard with favor; peace returned
Home to my breast, and to my memory
His promise, that your seed shall bruise our Foe;
Which then, not minded in dismay, yet now
Assures me that the bitterness of death
Is past, and we shall live. So hail to you,
Eve, rightly called the mother of mankind,
Mother of all things living, since by you
Man is to live, and all things live for Man.”
To whom thus Eve, with sad demeanor meek:
“Ill-suited that such title should belong
To me, transgressor, who, ordained for you
A help, became your snare; to me reproach
Rather belongs, distrust, and all dispraise.
But infinite in pardon was my Judge,
That I, who first brought death on all, am graced
The source of life; next favorable you,
Who highly thus to title me have deigned,
Far other name deserving. But the field
To labor calls us now, with sweat imposed,
Though after sleepless night; for see, the morn,
All unconcerned with our unrest, begins
Her rosy progress smiling; let us go;
I never from your side henceforth will stray,
Wherever lies our work, though now enjoined
Laborious, till day droops; while here we dwell,
What can be toilsome in these pleasant walks?
Here let us live, though fallen, still content.”
So spoke, so wished much-humbled Eve; but Fate
Assented not; first Nature gave signs, impressed
On bird, beast, air; air suddenly eclipsed
After short blush of morn; and in her sight
The bird of Jove, stooped from his airy round,
Two birds of brightest plume before him drove;
Down from a hill the beast that reigns in woods,
First hunter then, pursued a gentle brace,
Goodliest of all the forest, hart and hind;
Straight toward the eastern gate they bent their flight.
Adam observed, and, with his eye the chase
Pursuing, not unmoved, to Eve thus spoke:
“O Eve, some further change is close at hand,
Which Heaven by these mute signs in nature shows,
Forerunners of his purpose, or to warn
Us, perhaps too secure of our discharge
From penalty, because from death set free
Some days; how long, and what till then our life,
Who knows, or more than this, that we are dust,
And must return to it, and be no more?
Why else this double object in our sight,
Of flight pursued in air and over ground,
One way, the selfsame hour? Why in the east
Darkness before midday, and morning light
More orient in that western cloud that draws
Across the blue expanse a radiant white,
And slow descends, with something heavenly laden?”
He erred not; for by this the heavenly bands
Down from a sky of jasper lighted now
In Paradise, and on a hill made halt,
A glorious apparition, had not doubt
And carnal fear that day dimmed Adam’s eye.
Not that more glorious, when the angels met
Jacob in Mahanaim, where he saw
The field pavilioned with his guardians bright;
Nor that which on the flaming mount appeared
In Dothan, covered with a camp of fire,
Against the Syrian king, who, to surprise
One man, assassin-like had levied war,
War unproclaimed. The princely Hierarch
In their bright stand there left his Powers to seize
Possession of the garden; he alone,
To find where Adam sheltered, took his way,
Not unperceived by Adam, who to Eve,
While the great Visitant approached, thus spoke:
“Eve, now expect great tidings, which perhaps
Will soon determine for us, or impose
New laws to be observed; for I make out
From out that blazing cloud that veils the hill
One of the heavenly host, and by his gait
None of the meanest, some great potentate
Or of the Thrones above, such majesty
Invests him coming; yet not terrible,
That I should fear, nor sociably mild,
As Raphael, that I should much confide,
But solemn and sublime; whom, not to offend,
With reverence I must meet, and you withdraw.”
He ended; and the Archangel soon drew near,
Not in his shape celestial, but as man
Clad to meet man; over his lucid arms
A military vest of purple flowed,
Livelier than Meliboean, or the dye
Of Sarra, worn by kings and heroes old
In time of truce; Iris had dipped the cloth;
His starry helm, unbuckled, showed him prime
In manhood where youth ended; by his side,
As in a glittering zodiac, hung the sword,
Satan’s dire dread, and in his hand the spear.
Adam bowed low; he, kingly, from his state
Inclined not, but his coming thus declared:
“Adam, Heaven’s high command no preface needs:
Sufficient that your prayers are heard, and Death,
Then due by sentence when you first transgressed,
Defeated of his seizure many days
Given you of grace, in which you may repent,
And one bad act with many deeds well done
May cover: well may then your Lord, appeased,
Redeem you quite from Death’s rapacious claims;
But longer in this Paradise to dwell
Permits not; to remove you I have come,
And send you from the garden forth to till
The ground you were taken from, fitter soil.”
He said no more; for Adam at the news
Heart-struck with chilling grip of sorrow stood,
That all his senses bound; Eve, who unseen
Yet all had heard, with audible lament
Revealed soon the place of her retreat:
“O unexpected stroke, worse than of Death!
Must I thus leave you, Paradise? thus leave
You, native soil, these happy walks and shades,
Fit haunt of gods? where I had hoped to spend,
Quiet though sad, the respite of that day
That must be mortal to us both. O flowers,
That never will in other climate grow,
My early visitation, and my last
At evening, which I raised with tender hand
From the first opening bud, and gave you names,
Who now shall rear you to the sun, or rank
Your tribes, and water from the ambrosial fount?
You, lastly, nuptial bower, by me adorned
With what to sight or smell was sweet, from you
How shall I part, and where now wander down
Into a lower world, to this obscure
And wild? how shall we breathe in other air
Less pure, accustomed to immortal fruits?”
Whom thus the Angel interrupted, mild:
“Lament not, Eve, but patiently resign
What justly you have lost; nor set your heart,
Thus overfond, on that which is not yours.
Your going is not lonely; with you goes
Your husband; him to follow you are bound;
Where he abides, think there your native soil.”
Adam by this, from the cold sudden damp
Recovering, and his scattered spirits returned,
To Michael thus his humble words addressed:
“Celestial, whether among the Thrones, or named
Of them the highest, for such of shape may seem
Prince above princes, gently have you told
Your message, which might else in telling wound,
And in performing end us; what besides
Of sorrow and dejection and despair
Our frailty can sustain, your tidings bring:
Departure from this happy place, our sweet
Recess, and only consolation left
Familiar to our eyes; all places else
Inhospitable appear and desolate,
Nor knowing us nor known. And if by prayer
Incessant I could hope to change the will
Of him who can do all, I would not cease
To weary him with my assiduous cries;
But prayer against his absolute decree
No more avails than breath against the wind,
Blown stifling back on him that breathes it forth;
Therefore to his great bidding I submit.
This most afflicts me, that, in leaving here,
As from his face I shall be hid, deprived
His blessed presence; here I could frequent,
With worship, place by place where he vouchsafed
Presence divine, and to my sons relate:
‘On this mount he appeared; under this tree
Stood visible; among these pines his voice
I heard; here with him at this fountain talked.’
So many grateful altars I would raise
Of grassy turf, and pile up every stone
Of luster from the brook, in memory,
Or monument to ages, and on them
Offer sweet-smelling gums, and fruits, and flowers.
In that low world beneath, where shall I seek
His bright appearances, or footstep trace?
For though I fled him angry, yet, recalled
To life prolonged and promised race, I now
Gladly behold though but his utmost skirts
Of glory, and far off his steps adore.”
To whom thus Michael with regard benign:
“Adam, you know Heaven’s his, and all the earth,
Not this rock only; his omnipresence fills
Land, sea, and air, and every kind that lives,
Fostered by his effectual power, and warmed.
All earth he gave you to possess and rule,
No despicable gift; surmise not then
His presence to these narrow bounds confined
Of Paradise or Eden: this had been
Perhaps your capital seat, from which had spread
All generations, and had journeyed here
From all the ends of the earth, to celebrate
And reverence you, their great progenitor.
But this preeminence you have lost, brought down
To dwell on level ground now with your sons:
Yet doubt not but in valley and in plain
God is as here, and will be found alike
Present, and of his presence many a sign
Still following you, still compassing you round
With goodness and paternal love, his face
Express, and of his steps the track divine.
Which that you may believe, and be confirmed,
Before you go from here, know I am sent
To show you what shall come in future days
To you and to your offspring; good with bad
Expect to hear, supernal grace contending
With sinfulness of men; thereby to learn
True patience, and to temper joy with fear
And pious sorrow, equally inured
By moderation either state to bear,
Prosperous or adverse: so you shall lead
Safest your life, and, best prepared, endure
Your mortal passage when it comes. Ascend
This hill; let Eve (for I have drenched her eyes)
Here sleep below, while you to foresight wake,
As once you slept, while she to life was formed.”
To whom thus Adam gratefully replied:
“Ascend; I follow you, safe guide, the path
You lead me, and to the hand of Heaven submit,
However chastening; to the evil turn
My breast, laid open, arming to overcome
By suffering, and earn rest from labor won,
If so I may attain.” So both ascend
In the visions of God. It was a hill,
Of Paradise the highest, from whose top
The hemisphere of earth in clearest view
Stretched out to amplest reach of prospect lay.
Not higher that hill, nor wider looking round,
On which for different cause the Tempter set
Our second Adam in the wilderness,
To show him all earth’s kingdoms and their glory.
His eye might there command wherever stood
City of old or modern fame, the seat
Of mightiest empire, from the destined walls
Of Cambalu, seat of Cathayan Khan,
And Samarkand by Oxus, Timur’s throne,
To Paquin of Sinaean kings, and on
To Agra and Lahore of great Mogul,
Down to the golden Chersonese, or where
The Persian in Ecbatan sat, or since
In Ispahan, or where the Russian Czar
In Moscow, or the Sultan in Byzance,
Turkestan-born; nor could his eye not see
The Negus’ empire to his farthest port,
Ercoco, and the lesser coastal kings,
Mombasa, and Quiloa, and Melind,
And Sofala, thought Ophir, to the realm
Of Congo, and Angola farthest south;
Or from the Niger’s flood to Atlas Mount
The kingdoms of Almansor, Fez and Sus,
Morocco and Algiers, and Tremisen;
On Europe then, and where Rome was to sway
The world: in spirit perhaps he also saw
Rich Mexico, the seat of Montezuma,
And Cusco in Peru, the richer seat
Of Atabalipa, and yet unspoiled
Guiana, whose great city Geryon’s sons
Call El Dorado. But to nobler sights
Michael from Adam’s eyes the film removed
Which that false fruit that promised clearer sight
Had bred; then purged with euphrasy and rue
The visual nerve, for he had much to see;
And from the Well of Life three drops instilled.
So deep the power of these ingredients pierced,
Even to the inmost seat of mental sight,
That Adam, now compelled to close his eyes,
Sank down, and all his spirits became entranced;
But him the gentle Angel by the hand
Soon raised, and his attention thus recalled:
“Adam, now open your eyes, and first behold
The effects which your original crime has wrought
In some to spring from you, who never touched
The excepted tree, nor with the snake conspired,
Nor sinned your sin, yet from that sin derive
Corruption to bring forth more violent deeds.”
His eyes he opened, and beheld a field,
Part arable and tilled, on which were sheaves
New reaped, the other part sheep walks and folds;
In the midst an altar as the landmark stood,
Rustic, of grassy sod; there presently
A sweaty reaper from his tillage brought
First fruits, the green ear, and the yellow sheaf,
Unculled, as came to hand; a shepherd next,
More meek, came with the firstlings of his flock,
Choicest and best; then, sacrificing, laid
The inwards and their fat, with incense strewed,
On the cleft wood, and all due rites performed.
His offering soon propitious fire from Heaven
Consumed with nimble glance, and grateful steam;
The other’s not, for his was not sincere;
At which he raged within, and, as they talked,
Struck him into the midriff with a stone
That beat out life; he fell, and, deadly pale,
Groaned out his soul with gushing blood poured forth.
Much at that sight was Adam in his heart
Dismayed, and thus in haste to the Angel cried:
“O Teacher, some great mischief has befallen
That meek man, who had rightly sacrificed;
Is piety thus and pure devotion paid?”
To whom thus Michael, also moved, replied:
“These two are brothers, Adam, and to come
Out of your loins; the unjust has slain the just,
For envy that his brother’s offering found
From Heaven acceptance; but the bloody deed
Will be avenged, and the other’s faith, approved,
Lose no reward, though here you see him die,
Rolling in dust and gore.” To which our Sire:
“Alas, both for the deed and for the cause!
But have I now seen Death? Is this the way
I must return to native dust? O sight
Of terror, foul and ugly to behold,
Horrid to think, how horrible to feel!”
To whom thus Michael: “Death you have now seen
In his first shape on man; but many shapes
Of Death, and many are the ways that lead
To his grim cave, all dismal; yet to sense
More terrible at the entrance than within.
Some, as you saw, by violent stroke shall die,
By fire, flood, famine; by intemperance more
In meats and drinks, which on the earth shall bring
Diseases dire, of which a monstrous crew
Before you shall appear, that you may know
What misery the inabstinence of Eve
Shall bring on men.” Immediately a place
Before his eyes appeared, sad, noisome, dark;
A lazar house it seemed, in which were laid
Numbers of all diseased, all maladies
Of ghastly spasm, or racking torture, qualms
Of heartsick agony, all feverous kinds,
Convulsions, epilepsies, fierce catarrhs,
Stone in the bowels, ulcer, colic pangs,
Demonic frenzy, moping melancholy,
And moon-struck madness, pining atrophy,
Marasmus, and wide-wasting pestilence,
Dropsies, and asthmas, and joint-racking rheums.
Dire was the tossing, deep the groans; despair
Tended the sick, busiest from couch to couch;
And over them triumphant Death his dart
Shook, but delayed to strike, though often begged
With vows, as their chief good and final hope.
Sight so deformed what heart of rock could long
Dry-eyed behold? Adam could not, but wept,
Though not of woman born; compassion quelled
His best of man, and gave him up to tears
A space, till firmer thoughts restrained excess,
And, scarce recovering words, his plaint renewed:
“O miserable mankind, to what fall
Degraded, to what wretched state reserved!
Better end here unborn. Why is life given
To be thus wrested from us? rather, why
Obtruded on us thus? who, if we knew
What we receive, would either not accept
Life offered, or soon beg to lay it down,
Glad to be so dismissed in peace. Can thus
The image of God in man, created once
So goodly and erect, though faulty since,
To such unsightly sufferings be debased
Under inhuman pains? Why should not man,
Retaining still divine similitude
In part, from such deformities be free,
And for his Maker’s image be exempt?”
“Their Maker’s image,” answered Michael, “then
Forsook them, when themselves they vilified
To serve ungoverned appetite, and took
His image whom they served, a brutish vice,
That chiefly brought about the sin of Eve.
Therefore so abject is their punishment,
Disfiguring not God’s likeness, but their own,
Or if his likeness, by themselves defaced
While they pervert pure nature’s healthful rules
To loathsome sickness; worthily, since they
God’s image did not reverence in themselves.”
“I grant it just,” said Adam, “and submit.
But is there yet no other way, besides
These painful passages, for us to come
To death, and mix with our connatural dust?”
“There is,” said Michael, “if you well observe
The rule of not too much, by temperance taught
In what you eat and drink, seeking from it
Due nourishment, not gluttonous delight,
Till many years over your head return:
So may you live, till like ripe fruit you drop
Into your mother’s lap, or be with ease
Gathered, not harshly plucked, for death mature.
This is old age; but then you must outlive
Your youth, your strength, your beauty, which will change
To withered, weak, and gray; your senses then,
Obtuse, all taste of pleasure must forgo,
Compared to now; and, for the air of youth,
Hopeful and cheerful, in your blood will reign
A melancholy damp of cold and dry
To weigh your spirits down, and last consume
The balm of life.” To whom our Ancestor:
“Henceforth I flee not death, nor would prolong
Life much, bent rather how I may be quit,
Fairest and easiest, of this cumbrous charge,
Which I must keep till my appointed day
Of rendering up, and patiently attend
My dissolution.” Michael then replied:
“Nor love your life, nor hate; but what you live
Live well; how long or short, permit to Heaven.
And now make ready for another sight.”
He looked, and saw a spacious plain, on which
Were tents of various hue; by some were herds
Of cattle grazing; others, where the sound
Of instruments that made melodious chime
Was heard, of harp and organ; and who moved
Their stops and chords was seen: his flying touch,
Inspired through all proportions, low and high,
Fled and pursued transverse the resonant fugue.
In other part stood one who, at the forge
Toiling, two massive clods of iron and brass
Had melted (whether found where casual fire
Had wasted woods on mountain or in vale,
Down to the veins of earth, then gliding hot
To some cave’s mouth, or whether washed by stream
From underground); the liquid ore he drained
Into fit molds prepared; from which he formed
First his own tools; then what might else be wrought,
Cast or engraved in metal. After these,
But on this nearer side, a different sort
From the high neighboring hills, which were their seat,
Down to the plain descended: by their bearing
Just men they seemed, and all their study bent
To worship God aright, and know his works
Not hid, nor those things lost which might preserve
Freedom and peace to men. They on the plain
Long had not walked, when from the tents, behold,
A bevy of fair women, richly gay
In gems and wanton dress; to the harp they sang
Soft amorous songs, and in the dance came on.
The men, though grave, eyed them, and let their eyes
Rove without rein, till in the amorous net
Fast caught, they liked, and each his liking chose;
And now of love they treat till the evening star,
Love’s harbinger, appeared; then, all in heat,
They light the nuptial torch, and bid invoke
Hymen, then first to marriage rites invoked;
With feast and music all the tents resound.
Such happy interview and fair event
Of love and youth not lost, songs, garlands, flowers,
And charming symphonies, attached the heart
Of Adam, soon inclined to admit delight,
The bent of nature; which he thus expressed:
“True opener of my eyes, prime Angel blessed,
Much better seems this vision, and more hope
Of peaceful days portends, than those two past;
Those were of hate and death, or pain much worse;
Here nature seems fulfilled in all her ends.”
To whom thus Michael: “Judge not what is best
By pleasure, though to nature seeming fit,
Created, as you are, to nobler end,
Holy and pure, conformity divine.
Those tents you saw so pleasant were the tents
Of wickedness, in which shall dwell his race
Who slew his brother; studious they appear
Of arts that polish life, inventors rare,
Unmindful of their Maker, though his Spirit
Taught them; but they his gifts acknowledged none.
Yet they a beauteous offspring shall beget;
For that fair female troop you saw, that seemed
Of goddesses, so blithe, so smooth, so gay,
Yet empty of all good in which consists
Woman’s domestic honor and chief praise;
Bred only and completed to the taste
Of lustful appetence, to sing, to dance,
To dress, and troll the tongue, and roll the eye.
To these that sober race of men, whose lives
Religious titled them the Sons of God,
Shall yield up all their virtue, all their fame,
Ignobly, to the wiles and to the smiles
Of these fair atheists, and now swim in joy
(And soon to swim at large), and laugh; for which
The world before long a world of tears must weep.”
To whom thus Adam, of short joy bereft:
“O pity and shame, that they who to live well
Entered so fair should turn aside to tread
Paths indirect, or in the midway faint!
But still I see the tenor of man’s woe
Holds on the same, from woman to begin.”
“From man’s effeminate slackness it begins,”
Said the Angel, “who should better hold his place
By wisdom, and superior gifts received.
But now prepare for yet another scene.”
He looked, and saw wide territory spread
Before him, towns, and rural works between,
Cities of men with lofty gates and towers,
Concourse in arms, fierce faces threatening war,
Giants of mighty bone and bold exploit;
Part wield their arms, part curb the foaming steed,
Single or in array of battle ranged,
Both horse and foot, nor idly mustering stood.
One way a picked band, on a raid, drives off
A herd of cattle, handsome steers and cows,
From a rich meadow ground; or fleecy flock,
Ewes and their bleating lambs, over the plain,
Their booty; scarce with life the shepherds flee,
But call in aid, which makes a bloody fray;
With cruel tournament the squadrons join;
Where cattle pastured late, now scattered lies
With carcasses and arms the bloodied field,
Deserted. Others to a city strong
Lay siege, encamped; by battery, scale, and mine,
Assaulting; others from the wall defend
With dart and javelin, stones and sulfurous fire;
On each hand slaughter and gigantic deeds.
In other part the sceptered heralds call
To council in the city gates; at once
Gray-headed men and grave, with warriors mixed,
Assemble, and harangues are heard, but soon
In factious opposition, till at last
Of middle age one rising, eminent
For wisdom, spoke at length of right and wrong,
Of justice, of religion, truth and peace,
And judgment from above: him old and young
Shouted down, and had seized with violent hands,
Had not a cloud come down and snatched him off
Unseen amid the throng: so violence
Proceeded, and oppression, and sword-law,
Through all the plain, and refuge none was found.
Adam was all in tears, and to his guide
Lamenting turned full sad: “O what are these,
Death’s ministers, not men, who thus deal death
Inhumanly to men, and multiply
Ten thousandfold the sin of him who slew
His brother; for of whom such massacre
Make they but of their brethren, men of men?
But who was that just man, whom, had not Heaven
Rescued, had in his righteousness been lost?”
To whom thus Michael: “These are the product
Of those ill-mated marriages you saw,
Where good with bad were matched, who of themselves
Abhor to join; and, by imprudence mixed,
Produce prodigious births of body or mind.
Such were these giants, men of high renown;
For in those days might only shall be admired,
And valor and heroic virtue called;
To overcome in battle, and subdue
Nations, and bring home spoils with infinite
Manslaughter, shall be held the highest pitch
Of human glory, and for glory done
Of triumph, to be styled great conquerors,
Patrons of mankind, gods, and sons of gods,
Destroyers better called, and plagues of men.
Thus fame shall be achieved, renown on earth,
And what most merits fame in silence hid.
But he the seventh from you, whom you beheld
The only righteous in a world perverse,
And therefore hated, therefore so beset
With foes for daring single to be just,
And utter odious truth, that God would come
To judge them with his saints: him the Most High,
Rapt in a balmy cloud with winged steeds,
Did, as you saw, receive, to walk with God
High in salvation and the climes of bliss,
Exempt from death; to show you what reward
Awaits the good, the rest what punishment;
Which now direct your eyes and soon behold.”
He looked, and saw the face of things quite changed:
The brazen throat of war had ceased to roar;
All now was turned to jollity and game,
To luxury and riot, feast and dance,
Marrying or prostituting, as befell,
Rape or adultery, where passing fair
Allured them; then from cups to civil brawls.
At length a reverend sire among them came,
And of their doings great dislike declared,
And testified against their ways; he often
Frequented their assemblies, wherever met,
Triumphs or festivals, and to them preached
Conversion and repentance, as to souls
In prison under judgments imminent:
But all in vain; which when he saw, he ceased
Contending, and removed his tents far off;
Then from the mountain hewing timber tall,
Began to build a vessel of huge bulk,
Measured by cubit, length, and breadth, and height,
Smeared round with pitch, and in the side a door
Contrived, and of provisions laid in large
For man and beast: when lo, a wonder strange!
Of every beast, and bird, and insect small
Came sevens, and pairs, and entered in, as taught
Their order; last the sire, and his three sons
With their four wives; and God made fast the door.
Meanwhile the south wind rose, and with black wings
Wide hovering, all the clouds together drove
From under heaven; the hills to their supply
Vapor, and exhalation dusk and moist,
Sent up full force; and now the thickened sky
Like a dark ceiling stood; down rushed the rain
Impetuous, and continued till the earth
No more was seen; the floating vessel swam
Uplifted, and secure, with its beaked prow
Rode tilting over the waves; all dwellings else
Flood overwhelmed, and them with all their pomp
Deep under water rolled; sea covered sea,
Sea without shore; and in their palaces,
Where luxury late reigned, sea monsters whelped
And stabled; of mankind, so numerous late,
All left, in one small hull, swam on, embarked.
How did you grieve then, Adam, to behold
The end of all your offspring, end so sad,
Depopulation! You another flood,
A flood of tears and sorrow, also drowned,
And sank you as your sons; till, gently raised
By the Angel, on your feet you stood at last,
Though comfortless, as when a father mourns
His children, all in view destroyed at once;
And scarce to the Angel uttered thus your plaint:
“O visions ill foreseen! Better had I
Lived ignorant of future; so had borne
My part of evil only, each day’s lot
Enough to bear; those now that were dispensed
The burden of many ages, on me light
At once, by my foreknowledge gaining birth
Abortive, to torment me before they are,
With thought that they must be. Let no man seek
Henceforth to be foretold what shall befall
Him or his children, evil he may be sure,
Which neither his foreknowing can prevent,
And he the future evil shall no less
In apprehension than in substance feel,
Grievous to bear. But that care now is past;
No man is left to warn: those few escaped
Famine and anguish will at last consume,
Wandering that watery desert. I had hope
When violence was ceased, and war on earth,
All would have then gone well, peace would have crowned
With length of happy days the race of man;
But I was far deceived; for now I see
Peace to corrupt no less than war to waste.
How comes it thus? Unfold, celestial Guide,
And whether here the race of man will end.”
To whom thus Michael: “Those whom last you saw
In triumph and luxurious wealth are they
First seen in acts of prowess eminent
And great exploits, but of true virtue void;
Who, having spilled much blood, and done much waste
Subduing nations, and achieved thereby
Fame in the world, high titles, and rich prey,
Shall change their course to pleasure, ease, and sloth,
Surfeit, and lust, till wantonness and pride
Raise out of friendship hostile deeds in peace.
The conquered also, and enslaved by war,
Shall with their freedom lost all virtue lose,
And fear of God, from whom their piety feigned
In sharp contest of battle found no aid
Against invaders; therefore, cooled in zeal,
Thereafter shall learn how to live secure,
Worldly or dissolute, on what their lords
Shall leave them to enjoy; for the earth shall bear
More than enough, that temperance may be tried:
So all shall turn degenerate, all depraved,
Justice and temperance, truth and faith forgot;
One man except, the only son of light
In a dark age, against example good,
Against allurement, custom, and a world
Offended; fearless of reproach and scorn,
Or violence, he of their wicked ways
Shall them admonish, and before them set
The paths of righteousness, how much more safe,
And full of peace, proclaiming wrath to come
On their impenitence; and shall return
Of them derided, but of God observed
The one just man alive; by his command
Shall build a wondrous ark, as you beheld,
To save himself and household from amidst
A world condemned to universal wreck.
No sooner he, with them of man and beast
Select for life, shall in the ark be lodged,
And sheltered round, but all the cataracts
Of heaven set open on the earth shall pour
Rain day and night; all fountains of the deep,
Broke up, shall heave the ocean to usurp
Beyond all bounds, till inundation rise
Above the highest hills: then shall this mount
Of Paradise by might of waves be moved
Out of its place, pushed by the horned flood,
With all its verdure spoiled, and trees adrift,
Down the great river to the opening gulf,
And there take root, an island salt and bare,
The haunt of seals and orcs, and sea mews’ clang:
To teach you that God attributes to place
No sanctity, if none is carried there
By men who visit there, or there reside.
And now what further shall ensue, behold.”
He looked, and saw the ark drift on the flood,
Which now abated, for the clouds were fled,
Driven by a keen north wind, that, blowing dry,
Wrinkled the face of Deluge, as decayed;
And the clear sun on his wide watery glass
Gazed hot, and of the fresh wave largely drew,
As after thirst, which made their flowing shrink
From standing lake to tripping ebb, that stole
With soft foot toward the deep, who now had stopped
His sluices, as the heaven his windows shut.
The ark no more now floats, but seems on ground,
Fast on the top of some high mountain fixed.
And now the tops of hills as rocks appear;
With clamor then the rapid currents drive
Toward the retreating sea their furious tide.
At once from out the ark a raven flies,
And after him, the surer messenger,
A dove sent forth once and again to spy
Green tree or ground on which his foot may light;
The second time returning, in his bill
An olive leaf he brings, pacific sign:
And soon dry ground appears, and from his ark
The ancient sire descends with all his train;
Then with uplifted hands, and eyes devout,
Grateful to Heaven, over his head beholds
A dewy cloud, and in the cloud a bow
Conspicuous with three lifted colors gay,
Betokening peace from God, and covenant new.
At this the heart of Adam, late so sad,
Greatly rejoiced, and thus his joy broke forth:
“O you who future things can represent
As present, heavenly instructor, I revive
At this last sight, assured that man shall live,
With all the creatures, and their seed preserve.
Far less I now lament for one whole world
Of wicked sons destroyed, than I rejoice
For one man found so perfect and so just
That God vouchsafes to raise another world
From him, and all his anger to forget.
But say, what mean those colored streaks in heaven,
Distended as the brow of God appeased?
Or serve they as a flowery verge to bind
The fluid skirts of that same watery cloud,
Lest it again dissolve and shower the earth?”
To whom the Archangel: “Deftly have you aimed;
So willingly does God remit his wrath,
Though late repenting him of man depraved,
Grieved at his heart, when looking down he saw
The whole earth filled with violence, and all flesh
Corrupting each its way; yet, those removed,
Such grace shall one just man find in his sight
That he relents, not to blot out mankind,
And makes a covenant never to destroy
The earth again by flood, nor let the sea
Surpass its bounds, nor rain to drown the world
With man in it, or beast; but when he brings
Over the earth a cloud, will in it set
His triple-colored bow, on which to look
And call to mind his covenant: day and night,
Seedtime and harvest, heat and hoary frost
Shall hold their course, till fire purge all things new,
Both Heaven and Earth, in which the just shall dwell.”

blocks.p: Prevenient grace, sighs unutterable (3–6). Grace that comes before any human act and makes repentance possible; the new heart of flesh and the Spirit’s wordless groanings come from Scripture [Ezek. 11:19; Rom. 8:26].
Deucalion, Pyrrha, Themis (12–14). In Greek myth the only couple to survive Zeus’s flood, who prayed at the shrine of Themis, goddess of justice, to restore the human race.
golden altar, golden censer (18, 24). The altar of incense before God’s throne, where the prayers of the saints rise with the smoke [Rev. 8:3–4].
advocate, propitiation (33–34). Titles of Christ as the one who pleads for sinners and atones for their sins [1 John 2:1–2].
Horeb (74). The mountain where God came down in fire with a trumpet blast to give the Law [Exod. 19:16–19]; a trumpet will sound again at the Last Judgment [1 Thess. 4:16].
amaranthine (78). Of the amaranth, a legendary flower that never fades, here growing in Heaven.
like one of us (84). God’s words in Genesis on Man’s new knowledge and the Tree of Life [Gen. 3:22–23].
cherub watch, sword (120). The cherubim and flaming sword placed east of Eden [Gen. 3:24].
double Janus (129). The Roman god Janus had two faces; these cherubim have four, as in Ezekiel’s vision [Ezek. 1:6; 10:12].
Argus, Hermes (131–133). The hundred-eyed watchman of Greek myth, lulled to sleep by Hermes’ reed pipe and sleep-bringing wand, then slain.
Leucothea (135). “The white goddess,” a Greek sea goddess identified with Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn.
your seed shall bruise our Foe (155). God’s sentence on the serpent, read as the first promise of a redeemer [Gen. 3:15].
Mother of all things living (160). The meaning of Eve’s name [Gen. 3:20].
bird of Jove, beast that reigns in woods (185–188). The eagle, sacred to Jupiter, and the lion, now the first hunter since the Fall.
Mahanaim (214). Where the angels of God met Jacob, who named the place “two camps” [Gen. 32:1–2].
Dothan (217). Where the king of Syria sent an army to seize Elisha, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire [2 Kings 6:13–17].
Meliboean, Sarra, Iris (242–244). Meliboea in Thessaly and Sarra (Tyre) were famed for purple dye; Iris, goddess of the rainbow, had dyed the cloth.
second Adam in the wilderness (383–384). Christ, shown all the kingdoms of the world from a high mountain by Satan [Matt. 4:8; 1 Cor. 15:45].

Cambalu, Samarkand, Paquin, Agra, Lahore (388–391). Khanbalik (Beijing), seat of the Great Khan of Cathay; Samarkand on the Oxus, capital of Timur (Tamerlane); Peking of the Chinese (“Sinaean”) emperors; the Mughal capitals of India.
golden Chersonese (392). The Malay Peninsula, thought to be rich in gold.
Ecbatan, Ispahan, Byzance (393–395). Ancient and later capitals of Persia; Constantinople, ruled by Turkish sultans whose forebears came from Turkestan.

Negus, Ercoco, Sofala, Ophir (397–400). The emperor of Abyssinia and his Red Sea port of Arkiko; Mombasa, Kilwa (Quiloa), Malindi and Sofala were East African trading towns, Sofala thought by some to be Solomon’s gold land of Ophir [1 Kings 9:28].
Almansor, Sus, Tremisen (403–404). A Moorish ruler whose North African realm took in Fez, Sous and Tlemcen.

Atabalipa, Geryon’s sons (409–410). Atahualpa, the Inca emperor killed by the Spanish conquerors; the Spaniards are “Geryon’s sons” after a three-bodied giant of Spanish legend; El Dorado was the fabled city of gold.
euphrasy and rue (414). Herbs believed to clear the sight; euphrasy is eyebright.
lazar house (479). A hospital for lepers and the diseased poor, named for the beggar Lazarus [Luke 16:20].
catarrhs, rheums (483, 488). Inflammations of the nose and throat; watery discharges, especially of rheumatism.
Demonic frenzy ... pestilence (485–487). Lines Milton added in the 1674 edition; “moon-struck” madness was blamed on the moon’s influence, and marasmus is a wasting away of the body.
not of woman born (496). Adam was made from the dust, not born, yet weeps with a tenderness Milton’s age thought womanly.
cold and dry (544). In the old medicine, the qualities of the melancholy humor, which governs old age.
My dissolution (551–552). Milton’s 1674 expansion of this line; “dissolution” means death.
harp and organ, the forge (560–564). Jubal, “father of all who play the harp and organ,” and Tubal-cain, the first smith, both of Cain’s line [Gen. 4:20–22].
Hymen (591). The Greek god of marriage, called on at weddings.
Sons of God (622). Milton follows the reading that they were the godly line of Seth, who married women of Cain’s race [Gen. 6:1–2].
giants (642, 688). The Nephilim, “mighty men of old, men of renown” [Gen. 6:4].

one rising, the seventh from you (665, 700). Enoch, seventh from Adam, who prophesied that the Lord would come with his saints, and whom God took [Jude 14–15; Gen. 5:24]; the cloud and winged steeds recall Elijah’s chariot [2 Kings 2:11].
reverend sire (719). Noah, “a preacher of righteousness” [2 Pet. 2:5]; the “souls in prison” echo [1 Pet. 3:19–20].
horned flood, orcs, sea mews (831–835). A river was pictured with horns, for its branching mouths or its roar; orcs are whales or sea monsters, sea mews are gulls.
bow, covenant (865–898). The rainbow sign of God’s promise never again to destroy the earth by flood [Gen. 8:22; 9:11–17].
fire purge all things new (900). The burning and renewal of Heaven and Earth at the end of the age [2 Pet. 3:10–13].
